title: When Your Teacher Is a Bot
author: Will Austin
summary: Austin, a former teacher and principal who founded Boston Schools Fund, assesses Alpha School's arrival in Beacon Hill, Jamaica Plain and Lexington and concludes the model will neither work nor spread. He separates his position from technophobia, granting that AI already helps with scheduling, disability paperwork and multilingual support, and arguing technology earns its place when it raises productivity rather than engagement. His empirical objection is specific: when Alpha's model was tested through a lottery-admission public charter in Arizona, called Unbound Academy, achievement was low, which suggests the chain's results come from admissions rather than instruction. His deeper disagreement is conceptual. Racing to learn content efficiently misses what primary education is for, since the specific facts fade while the capacity to learn persists, and he cites a study of Chinese students who used AI tools to finish homework faster and more accurately but performed worse on tests. He also punctures the personal-tutor framing, noting that what Alpha actually delivers is a guide and a room of Chromebooks rather than Socrates. The closing arithmetic is a scalability argument: at least three times per-pupil spending for at most 180 students in a system serving 900,000.
points: Uses Alpha's own Arizona lottery-admission charter, where achievement was low, as the cleanest available test that the model's results come from selection rather than teaching.
Draws a line between technology as a productivity tool in school operations and technology as a replacement for curriculum, instruction and assessment.
Argues the efficiency framing misunderstands primary education, since adults retain the meta-skill of learning rather than the specific content they once knew.
Cites research on Chinese students finishing homework faster and more accurately with AI while scoring worse on tests, as evidence that struggle is part of learning.
Frames the model as fundamentally unscalable, charging at least three times Massachusetts per-pupil spending to serve at most 180 students in Greater Boston.
quotes: Founded in 2014 in Texas, Alpha School is a rapidly expanding chain of private schools in which children engage with AI-enabled software and chatbots, all monitored by an adult “guide” instead of a teacher.

I am not a Luddite; technology has been an incredible force for good in education. From simple innovations like electronic chalkboards to automated assessments and data analysis, technology in schools is at its best when it is a driver of productivity, not a gimmick or an engagement vehicle.
When its model was rigorously tested after opening a public charter school called Unbound Academy in Arizona, it didn’t work: Student achievement results were quite low.
That suggests that the secret to its success is admissions, not classroom practice: Serving higher-income students led to higher “outcomes.

Few educated adults can tell you what a gerundive is, how to complete the square, or who Abraham Lincoln’s first vice president was. But we did know those things at some point. That is because we learned how to learn, not just memorize, a meta-skill that we employ constantly in our personal and professional lives as adults. Details fade, but concepts stay.

A new study bears this out. It found that Chinese middle and high school students who relied on AI tools finished their homework more accurately and quickly, but did worse on tests. Learning requires attention, struggle, time, even touch. ChatGPT can’t do that for you.
Fair, but Alpha School is not offering Socrates. You get a guide and a room with kids full of Chromebooks.
And, in that way, there is nothing truly new about Alpha School. It is just the AI update for the long tradition of small, exclusive schools that cater to families with means.
